title: Linear versus general resolution
formal:
Is linear resolution strictly weaker than general resolution in polynomial refutation size, for the same input CNF formula? Here linear resolution has no restarts, and the size \(\ell\) is one plus the number of resolution inferences. More precisely, is the following assertion true?
\[
\forall c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_0\
\exists F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\ \exists\pi\
\left[
\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\ \land\
\forall\lambda\
\left(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\Longrightarrow
\ell(\lambda)>c\,\ell(\pi)^{k}\right)
\right].
\]
The classes of formulas and the two syntactic refutation predicates are defined below. This asserts failure of every polynomial bound on the extra proof length needed by linear resolution. The constants \(c,k\) range independently over positive integers; \(n,F,\pi\) may depend on them. The comparison concerns existence of proofs, with no requirement that a conversion between proofs be computable in polynomial time. It does not prescribe an exponential separation or an effectively generated family of formulas.
why: This compares two longstanding, complete refinements of a foundational propositional proof system. It isolates the effect of how deductions are organized and reused, with the inference rule and input formula held fixed. A separation would identify an intrinsic proof-length cost of the linear discipline; a polynomial simulation would show that arbitrary resolution structure can always be reproduced within polynomial length. The result would clarify the strength hierarchy of resolution refinements, independently of how efficiently a solver can discover the proofs.

Both outcomes identify what proof reuse and deduction order can accomplish. Its breadth is substantially greater than a bound for one formula family; the score reflects that foundational role, not practical use of linear resolution in current SAT solvers or merely the age of the question. This replaces the explicitly unassessed midpoint 50.

sentences: General resolution refutes a Boolean CNF by combining and reusing clauses in an arbitrary acyclic proof.
Linear resolution without restarts keeps one main chain, using the preceding clause together with an input clause or an earlier main clause at every inference.
The question asks whether this restriction causes a superpolynomial increase in refutation length on some formulas, with length counted by resolution inferences.
The source definition requires an explicit correction to exclude restarts, and the bounded later review found no verified resolution of the intended same-formula comparison.
A complete Lean answer must prove either failure of every polynomial size bound or one universal polynomial simulation, without an extra requirement to find the converted proofs efficiently.

definitions:
For \(n\in\mathbb N_0\), put \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\), for \(i\in[n]\). A clause is a finite set of literals containing at most one of \(x_i,\neg x_i\) for each \(i\); thus all clauses are non-tautological and repeated literals are identified. A formula \(F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\) is a finite set of clauses, interpreted as their conjunction. A valuation \(v:[n]\to\{0,1\}\) makes \(x_i\) true when \(v(i)=1\) and makes \(\neg x_i\) true when \(v(i)=0\). A clause is true if it contains a true literal. The empty clause \(\varnothing\) is false, while the empty conjunction is true. A formula is unsatisfiable if no valuation makes all its clauses true.

The sole inference rule is resolution. If \(i\in[n]\), neither \(x_i\) nor \(\neg x_i\) occurs in clauses \(A,B\), and \(A\cup B\) is non-tautological, the rule is
\[
\frac{A\cup\{x_i\}\qquad B\cup\{\neg x_i\}}{A\cup B}.
\]
The two premises may be interchanged. The variable \(x_i\) is the pivot. Every input and derived clause uses variables in \([n]\). There is no weakening rule, additional axiom, introduction of a new variable, or permission to add tautological clauses. Equality of clauses is equality of their literal sets.

A general resolution refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\) is a finite nonempty directed acyclic graph of clause occurrences with one sink, labelled \(\varnothing\). Every vertex reaches that sink. Each source vertex is labelled by a clause of \(F\); every other vertex has exactly two parent vertices and is labelled by the resolvent of their labels under the displayed rule. Each such vertex records its pivot and premise orientation. A clause occurrence may be used as a parent arbitrarily many times. Distinct vertices may have equal labels. This defines \(\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\). A single vertex labelled \(\varnothing\) is allowed exactly when \(\varnothing\in F\).

A linear resolution refutation \(\lambda\) of \(F\) is a finite main sequence
\[
C_0,C_1,\ldots,C_t,\qquad
t\in\mathbb N_0,\quad C_0\in F,\quad C_t=\varnothing,
\]
together with the following annotations. For every integer \(j\) with \(0\le j<t\), the next clause \(C_{j+1}\) is the resolvent of \(C_j\) and a side clause \(D_j\). The side clause is either an input clause \(D_j\in F\), or an earlier main clause \(D_j=C_i\) for a specified integer \(i\) with \(0\le i<j\). The annotation records which alternative is used, its clause or index, and the pivot and premise orientation. This defines \(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\).

Every step after the first main clause must therefore use the immediately preceding main clause as a premise. One cannot insert a new input clause as the next main clause without deriving it by that rule: such an insertion would be a restart. An input clause can nevertheless be used as a side clause whenever needed, whether or not it appeared previously in the main sequence. Earlier main clauses can be reused as side clauses without a limit on the number of uses. All such earlier main clauses are ancestors of the current main clause along the main sequence; no further ancestor test is imposed. Side clauses are not restricted to input clauses. There is no regularity requirement forbidding repeated use of a pivot along a proof path, and no subsumption requirement that a conclusion be contained in its preceding main clause.

For either type of refutation, define
\[
\ell(\Pi)=1+\text{the number of resolution inferences in }\Pi.
\]
Thus \(\ell(\pi)\) for a general refutation is one plus its number of non-source vertices, and \(\ell(\lambda)=t+1\) for the displayed linear refutation. Reusing a parent is not a new inference; deriving a new occurrence is. Input clauses used as side premises do not themselves count as resolution inferences. The additive one includes a refutation with no inference. This is a count of deductions, not the binary length of the whole formula or of its serialized proof.

For a finite representation, label variables by their integer indices, store clauses as sorted lists of signed indices without repetitions, and store formulas as sorted lists of distinct clauses. In a general proof, index vertices in a topological order and store their clause labels and source or two-parent annotations; in a linear proof store the main sequence and its side-clause annotations. All integer indices have ordinary finite binary encodings. These representations specify finite proof objects; the cost remains \(\ell\), without charging literal, index or annotation bits. The same \(F\) must be used in both proof systems. No formula transformation, additional input clause, width bound, clause bound, or proof-search time bound is part of the comparison.

In this card, polynomial simulation means that there are single constants \(c,k\ge1\) such that every general refutation of every \(F\) has some linear refutation of that same \(F\) of size at most \(c\,\ell(\pi)^k\). This is ordinary proof-size simulation. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm producing the latter proof would be the stronger notion of \(p\)-simulation and is not required here. Every linear refutation is a particular general refutation when its main and input occurrences are represented as a graph, so only the converse simulation is at issue.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the assertion in the formal statement or of its full negation, using exactly the formulas, inference rule, proof predicates and size measure above.

A positive answer must show that for every pair \(c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), there is a finite formula with a general refutation \(\pi\) for which every linear refutation has size greater than \(c\,\ell(\pi)^k\), with all the quantifiers of the displayed assertion. No particular exponential rate or uniformly generated counterexample family is required.

A negative answer must prove the polynomial simulation statement
\[
\exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_0\
\forall F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\ \forall\pi\
\left[
\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\Longrightarrow
\exists\lambda\
\left(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\land
\ell(\lambda)\le c\,\ell(\pi)^k\right)
\right].
\]
The same \(c,k\) must work for every formula and every general refutation; the linear refutation may depend on the formula and proof. An efficient proof-conversion algorithm would suffice if its size guarantee meets this statement, but is not an additional obligation. Comparisons allowing restarts, changing the input formula, using resolution over linear equations, or imposing extra regularity or input-only restrictions do not answer the stated question. A separation at one fixed polynomial degree also does not prove the universal separation assertion. This is a yes/no comparison of asymptotic proof lengths, so numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not alter the quantifiers or polynomial bounds.

context_blocks.text: Nordström's 2013 survey poses the unresolved strength comparison in Section 3.2. Its preceding definition permits restarting the main sequence from an input clause. This card preserves the intended open question while explicitly correcting that definition to linear resolution without restarts, using the later direct definition of Buss and Johannsen.

Buss and Johannsen distinguish the two systems: allowing restarts gives a polynomial-time simulation of general resolution, whereas the strength of linear resolution without restarts remains open in their account. They also prove that regular resolution does not simulate linear resolution; that different comparison does not settle the question here.

Johannsen's 2018 Dagstuhl contribution again gives the no-restarts definition and asks about superpolynomial separation or polynomial-time simulation of unrestricted resolution. This card fixes the original proof-size comparison, distinguishing ordinary polynomial simulation from the additional efficient-conversion requirement in the latter alternative.

An ECCC correction dated November 2002 withdraws the earlier claimed separation: its author identifies a failed lemma and unproved separation theorems. The old report title must therefore not be treated as a solution of this problem.

The later primary results checked in the bounded review include effective simulation, which permits changing the input formula, and a separation for resolution over parity equations. Their models differ from the unchanged-formula, classical-clause comparison in this card.

Read the actual Nordstrom arXiv1307.3913v3 PDF (20 September 2013), Section 3.2, printed/PDF21–22. The definition on p. 21 permits a clause in the main sequence to be a fresh input axiom at any point; this is precisely the restart allowance distinguished by Buss–Johannsen. The p. 22 unresolved comparison cannot be read as a new open question about the restart-enabled system, since that system already polynomially simulates general resolution. The draft therefore makes the correction explicit and preserves the intended source question.

Read the actual LMU author-hosted Buss–Johannsen PDF, including pp. 1–4, Theorem 8 p. 6, and the statements on pp. 8 and 10. It is labelled Preliminary version and has no printed revision date; PDF metadata gives 20 July 2017. The author's institutional publication page lists the article as JSAT 10, pp. 23–35 (2017), while some later bibliographies label it 2016. Record the exact checked preprint rather than claiming published-journal page locators. The UCSD copy had certificate/timeout errors and publisher retrieval did not produce a readable journal PDF.

Buss–Johannsen assumes non-tautological clauses throughout on p. 2. Definition 1 p. 3 allows an arbitrary input side clause or an earlier main clause, but no restart after the initial clause. It imposes neither regularity nor the extra subsumption condition of its separate s-linear system. The earlier-main alternative includes arbitrary reuse; input-only resolution would be a different, more restricted system. The general DAG presentation immediately following Definition 2 on p. 3 has input sources, binary resolution vertices and a single conclusion sink. Ordinary resolution introduces neither new variables nor extra axioms.

Definition 4 and its remark on p. 4 distinguish ordinary polynomial size simulation from p-simulation, and distinguish their broader clause-derivation comparison from the traditional refutation-only definition. This draft fixes the original strength question as ordinary refutation-size simulation on the identical CNF, not the stronger all-conclusions/subclause comparison or an efficient conversion requirement. Size is number of inferences as in that definition, normalized to one plus the count to handle an input empty clause. Counting all source occurrences as well gives a constant-factor comparable measure for a connected binary refutation; no claim of exact equality to serialized bit length is used.

Read the actual Dagstuhl Reports publisher PDF for Seminar 18051, Section 4.5.1 printed p. 150/PDF27 and Section 4.5.2 Open Problem 11 printed p. 151/PDF28. Johannsen directly restates the no-restarts definition and the longstanding separation/simulation question. The report was published 20 July 2018. Its p-simulation alternative is stronger than the ordinary-size negation in this card; these notions are explicitly distinguished rather than asserted equivalent. The cited bibliography's volume/year inconsistencies do not override the exact downloaded Buss–Johannsen edition.

Read Buss–Yolcu arXiv2402.15871v1, submitted 24 February 2024 (title-page date 27 February), abstract, Definition 1.1 pp. 1–2, listed simulations p. 2, and Theorem 3.1 p. 3. Effective simulation permits transforming the input CNF. Its stated linear-resolution example and its new regular-resolution theorem therefore do not answer this card. The audit checked definitions and theorem scope, not the complete theorem proof.

Read the actual CCC2024 Article23 publisher PDF, published 15 July 2024, abstract and model on printed pp. 23:1–23:2. ResLin means resolution over affine equations over the two-element field; the result separates bottom-regular ResLin from general resolution and hence from general ResLin. It is not a separation between the classical main-chain linear system and general resolution. A 2025 resolution-over-parities tradeoff search hit was likewise not used as evidence of a solution to the classical linear question.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026 covered linear resolution, unrestricted/general resolution, refutation simulation and separation, exact open-question wording, and 2025/2026 results. Recent search results about commutative-algebra linear resolutions, spatial resolution, ResLin parity systems and formula-changing effective simulation were distinguished from this target. No verified exact solution was found; this is neither an exhaustive bibliography nor proof of current openness.

The formal assertion quantifies over every positive integer pair c,k and permits the finite counterexample formula and general proof to depend on them. Its full logical negation supplies one c,k for all formulas and all general refutations, with an existential linear refutation of the identical input. The statement does not demand a polynomial-size general proof as a function of a chosen family index, an explicit family, or a fixed exponential gap. All such extra requirements would strengthen the original ordinary non-simulation question.

No solver technique, proposed separation family, closure characterization or intermediate milestone is included in the public statement. Completeness is a dated source fact, while the Lean acceptance criterion remains the full comparison; no existing formal verification is claimed. The numerical tolerance rule does not apply as an additive error to the polynomial simulation statement.
